input.claim_text: On 3 February 2023 heavy rain caused the creek behind our property to overflow and water came into our home, ruining the carpets in the living room and soaking the bottom of the plasterboard walls. It happened really fast, within about an hour the water was ankle deep inside. We've had to rip up the carpet already because it started smelling. I think it'll cost around $9,000 to fix the flooring and walls.

output.cause: creek overflowed due to heavy rain
output.damaged_item: living room carpets and plasterboard walls

input.query: Flood damage coverage - creek overflow, is flood a covered peril or excluded?

output.answer:
Based on the excerpts provided, **Flood is a covered peril**, subject to specific exclusions.

**Definition of Flood:** Flood is defined as "the covering of normally dry land by water that has escaped or been released from the normal confines of: • any lake, or any river, creek or other natural watercourse, whether or not altered or modified; or • any reservoir, canal or dam" [RAA Contents PDS, page 87]. This definition explicitly includes creek overflow.

**Coverage:** Section 12 confirms "What we Cover for loss or damage to the Insured Property provide[d] as a result of Flood" [RAA Contents PDS, page 50].

**Exclusions that still apply even where Flood cover exists:**
- Loss or damage to any part of the Home not fully built
- Tennis courts
- Wharves, jetties, pontoons or sea walls
- Water in a tank, swimming pool or spa (and cleaning costs)
- Swimming pools/spas and their covers or liners (except permanently attached hard lid style pool covers)
- Paint damage where there is no accompanying structural damage from Flood
- Damage caused by underground (hydrostatic) water
- Glasshouses or greenhouses
- Unsealed paths or driveways (e.g., gravel or loose materials)
- Flood arising from deliberate or Malicious Damage to a reservoir or dam
- Paths/driveways (and other listed items, cut off in the excerpt) that were not structurally sound or reasonably maintained prior to the loss
[RAA Contents PDS, page 50]

**Additional exclusion from the definition itself:** Flood excludes water from Actions of the Sea, except where caused by a Storm Surge occurring at the same time as Storm damage, or a Tsunami; and it excludes any mixture of water from Actions of the Sea with water from another source [RAA Contents PDS, page 88].

**Conclusion:** For a creek overflow specifically, this falls squarely within the Flood definition [RAA Contents PDS, page 87], so damage from such an event would be covered under Section 12, unless one of the specific listed exclusions above applies (e.g., damage to a pool, unsealed driveway, or a not-structurally-sound path).

The excerpts do not include the full list of items under the final exclusion bullet (the text is cut off after "a driveway; –"), so I cannot confirm the complete list of additional exclusions in that section.

turns.text:
DECISION: approve

The claimed peril—creek overflow due to heavy rain flooding the home—falls squarely within RAA's policy definition of "Flood" ("the covering of normally dry land by water that has escaped or been released from the normal confines of any lake, or any river, creek or other natural watercourse...") [RAA Contents PDS, page 87], and Flood is an insured peril under Section 12 [RAA Contents PDS, page 50]. None of the listed carve-outs (unfinished structures, tennis courts, pools/spas, unsealed driveways, hydrostatic groundwater, paint-only damage, etc.) apply to this claim, which involves carpet and plasterboard wall damage from surface floodwater entering the home [RAA Contents PDS, page 50, page 88].

Policyholder's certificate figures: excess $500, coverage limit $45,000. Applying these to the claimed $9,000 repair estimate yields a payout of $8,500 ($9,000 − $500 excess), which is well within the coverage limit.

Sources cited:
[RAA Contents PDS, page 50]
[RAA Contents PDS, page 87]
[RAA Contents PDS, page 88]
